blocks.text: About two hundred million sperm cells begin the journey; one arrives. From that single fusion, nine months later, comes a baby with roughly two trillion cells, every one descended from that one zygote. Understanding this sequence is also the foundation of understanding family planning and sexually transmitted infections.

blocks.markdown:
## The male reproductive system

The **testes** lie in the **scrotum**, a sac of skin outside the body cavity. This position keeps them about two degrees below core body temperature, which sperm production requires. Inside each testis, coiled seminiferous tubules produce sperm by meiosis, and cells between the tubules secrete the hormone **testosterone**.

Sperm pass into the **epididymis**, where they mature and are stored, then along the **sperm duct (vas deferens)**. On the way, three glands add fluid: the **seminal vesicle**, the **prostate gland** and Cowpers gland. The fluid contains fructose to fuel the sperm and is alkaline to neutralise the acidity of the vagina. Sperm plus this fluid is **semen**. It leaves through the **urethra** in the **penis**.

A sperm cell is a specialist: a head containing the nucleus, capped by an enzyme-filled acrosome that digests a path into the egg; a middle piece packed with mitochondria for energy; and a long tail for swimming.

## The female reproductive system

The two **ovaries** contain all the potential egg cells a woman will ever have. Each month one **ovum** is released — **ovulation** — and is swept by cilia into the funnel of the **oviduct (fallopian tube)**. The oviduct leads to the **uterus (womb)**, a muscular organ with a thick lining called the **endometrium**. The narrow neck of the uterus is the **cervix**, which opens into the **vagina**.

An ovum is far larger than a sperm, is non-motile, and contains food reserves in its cytoplasm.

blocks.caption: Reproductive structures and their functions

blocks.title: The menstrual cycle, day by day
blocks.prompt: Outline the events of a 28-day menstrual cycle and name the hormone controlling each phase.

steps.text: Days 1 to 5 — menstruation. The endometrium built up in the previous cycle breaks down and is shed with some blood through the vagina, because progesterone levels have fallen.
Days 1 to 13 — follicular phase. FSH from the pituitary stimulates a follicle in the ovary to develop. The growing follicle secretes oestrogen, which repairs and thickens the endometrium.
Around day 14 — ovulation. Rising oestrogen triggers a surge of LH from the pituitary, which causes the follicle to rupture and release the ovum into the oviduct.

Days 15 to 28 — luteal phase. The empty follicle becomes the corpus luteum and secretes progesterone, which maintains the thick endometrium ready for implantation and inhibits FSH so no new follicle develops.
If no fertilisation occurs, the corpus luteum degenerates by about day 26, progesterone falls, and the endometrium can no longer be maintained — so menstruation begins and the cycle repeats.

If fertilisation does occur, the developing embryo signals the corpus luteum to persist. Progesterone stays high, the endometrium is retained, and there is no menstruation — which is why a missed period is the first sign of pregnancy.

blocks.answer: Menstruation (days 1–5), follicle development under FSH with oestrogen thickening the endometrium (days 1–13), ovulation triggered by an LH surge (about day 14), then the corpus luteum secreting progesterone to maintain the lining (days 15–28).

blocks.markdown:
### Fertilisation, implantation and pregnancy

Sperm deposited in the vagina swim through the cervix and uterus into the oviduct. **Fertilisation** normally occurs in the upper oviduct: one sperm's acrosome digests through the egg membrane, its nucleus fuses with the egg nucleus, and the membrane immediately changes so no other sperm can enter. The **zygote** is diploid, with 46 chromosomes — 23 from each parent.

The zygote divides by mitosis as it travels down the oviduct, becoming a ball of cells. About a week after fertilisation it sinks into the endometrium: this is **implantation**, and from this point it is called an **embryo**. After about eight weeks, when the organs are recognisable, it is called a **foetus**.

The **placenta** develops where the embryo meets the uterine wall. It has a very large surface area of finger-like villi and brings the two bloodstreams extremely close together without mixing them. Oxygen, glucose, amino acids, mineral salts, water, vitamins and antibodies pass from mother to foetus; carbon dioxide and urea pass from foetus to mother. Keeping the bloodstreams separate matters, because the mother's blood pressure would damage the foetus and their blood groups may be incompatible.

Harmful substances can also cross the placenta, which is why alcohol, nicotine, some drugs and the viruses of rubella and HIV can reach and damage the foetus.

blocks.title: Gestation and birth
blocks.text: Gestation is the period of development inside the uterus — about 40 weeks, or nine months, in humans. At birth (parturition) the muscular uterine wall contracts rhythmically, the cervix dilates, the amnion ruptures releasing the amniotic fluid, and the baby is pushed out head first, followed by the placenta as the afterbirth.

blocks.title: Two facts examiners test relentlessly
blocks.text: Fertilisation occurs in the oviduct, not in the uterus or the ovary. And the mother's and foetus's blood never mix — they exchange materials by diffusion and active transport across the placenta. Getting either of these wrong costs marks in almost every paper.

points: The testes produce sperm and testosterone and hang in the scrotum to stay below body temperature.
The ovaries produce ova and the hormones oestrogen and progesterone; ovulation occurs about day 14 of the cycle.
FSH stimulates follicle development, oestrogen thickens the endometrium, an LH surge triggers ovulation and progesterone maintains the lining.
Fertilisation takes place in the oviduct, and implantation of the embryo takes place in the endometrium of the uterus.
The placenta exchanges materials by diffusion and active transport, but the maternal and foetal bloodstreams remain separate.
